explanation: Fires on tokens naming combat sports, martial arts, bladed/cutting implements, and winter board/skate sports: e.g. 'WBO', 'Street Fighter', 'Kung Fu', 'MMA', 'UFC', 'flyweight', 'punch', 'knife/knives', 'blades', 'scabbard', 'razors', 'snowboard', 'skates', 'skis'. Strongest for fighting/boxing terms and blades; weaker for unrelated gear (wok, equipment), and some name fragments fire weakly or moderately for no clear reason.

Fires strongly on a heterogeneous mix of tokens in technical, medical-academic and code/log contexts, often word-piece completions or compound terms (e.g. 'standardized mean difference', 'transurethral', 'autonomic', 'Dockerfile COPY', 'recaptcha', 'BasicCredentialsProvider', 'Staff Writer', 'may be reached'). No single shared semantic or lexical feature is evident.

Fires on content tokens inside dense technical, scientific, legal-license and code-import text (e.g. 'grant of patent rights', 'import Glibc', 'sys/cdefs.h', 'PropTypes from', 'chloride channels', 'fullerene', 'thermoelectric', 'lifetime license'), with lower activations on 'my' in casual text. The common thread is only a broad 'jargon-heavy technical/list context'; it is hard to predict individual tokens.

Fires mainly on the prefix token ' micro' at the start of a compound word (microgravity, microcontroller, microarray, microtransactions, microbubbles), and also on other word-initial prefix pieces such as 'ad' (Advising, adoration, adjudication, adapt), 'U' in 'Undefeated', 'Res' in 'Resurrection', and 'i' in 'i.e.'. Essentially detects the first sub-word piece of a word that will be continued, strongest for 'micro'.

Fires most strongly inside long runs of repeated characters or digits (e.g. '00000000000[5]', '0000000 +', '3333);', long ';;;;' runs), and moderately on mid-word fragments in hex hashes/IDs, rare-language subwords (German, Japanese) and on 'function/command' in programming Q&A titles. Main driver is repetitive/garbled character-string context.

Fires on tokens in reasoning or hypothesis-forming language, where a writer is posing a question, conjecture or explanation: 'Does that sound reasonable?', 'We hypothesize', 'supported the hypothesis', 'to explain the data', 'Am I missing something?', 'Can't be hard', 'Am I likely', also on targets in math-problem prompts ('the o'th term', 'solve for p', 'find the minimum'). Strongest at the word expressing the inference/question itself.

Fires on proper nouns and specialized named terms, especially brand/organization/person names and legal or medical terms (Comey, Kardashians, Oculus, NASCAR, AFC Wimbledon, Obamacare, NUnit, ComVisible, 'Civil' in Code of Civil Procedure, misdemeanor, celiac), plus garbled Devanagari bytes and 'assertEqual'. A loose 'distinctive named entity / term' detector with mixed members.

Fires most strongly inside long runs of repeated digits or symbols ('00000000000[5]', '0000000 +', '8888,', ';;;;' runs), and moderately on the keyword 'func' starting a top-level declaration in Go source (after a blank line), plus a few Go/Angular code tokens. Two jobs: repeated-character strings and Go function declarations.

Fires on a mixture of tokens with no clear common theme: mid-word pieces of foreign names and places (Suluk, Richelle, Csörnyei, Versailles, uilleann), ' a' in 'is a village in' gazetteer stubs, LaTeX/HTML syntax pieces ('{', '="', '/Web'), and technical modifiers ('vertical cavity', 'wide bandgap', 'posterior temporal').

Fires on the verb 'hope' (and nearby words) in friendly first-person addresses to a reader, typical of blog/website greetings and sign-offs ('I hope you have all had', 'We hope you found some useful', 'Hi, my name is', 'This is my first post', 'Thank you so much in advance'). Strongest on 'hope' after I/We in a reader-directed greeting; weaker on other conversational greeting tokens.

Fires on a broad mixture of tokens, often the first piece of a multi-token word (phon-on, Dop-pler, fantas-ist, felon-ies, HEL-LO, HOM-EPATH, pall-iation, Cond-ensate) but also ordinary words in fixed phrases ('on the one hand', 'Do the same', 'has more protons', 'one of the following'). No single predictable feature.

Fires on word-piece tokens inside non-English text (Dutch, French, German, Romanian, Spanish, Portuguese) and on first sub-word pieces of foreign place/proper names in English text (Kanagawa, Trieste, Balochistan, Mecca, Roraima, Bheem), plus some medical word starts ('vert-ebrae', 'contr-alateral'). Main job: sub-word pieces of foreign-language or foreign-name words.

Fires most strongly on LaTeX relation commands ('\equiv', '\simeq', '\geq' pieces) in math text, and moderately on ' the' after comparison/position prepositions ('below the', 'above the', 'member of the') and 'relative' in CSS 'position: relative'. Main job is mathematical relation/comparison operators, with comparative-position phrases as related offshoot.

Fires in conditional/restrictive clauses, especially the boilerplate 'if not' in GNU/BSD software license headers ('along with this program; if not, write to...'), and similar license terms ('commercial license', 'source code', 'military purposes'), plus other 'if/those that X' conditional contexts ('those that work today', 'If not, carry on'). Strongest on 'not' after 'if' in license text.
